The Pink ear emperor (Lethrinus lentjan) is a commercially important lethrinid species inhabiting coral reef ecosystems across the Indo-Pacific region. Field studies conducted in the Red Sea have documented the maximum total length achieved by this species, with individuals reaching an ultimate size of 52 cm [Li = 52 cm]. This asymptotic length is comparable to values reported for other medium-bodied emperors within the genus Lethrinus, reflecting the typical growth trajectory of this predatory fish under favorable environmental conditions. Marked individuals examined during long-term monitoring programs rarely exceed this threshold, indicating that growth slows considerably once this size is approached. The species demonstrates a relatively robust body form, with adults possessing the characteristic pinkish coloration on the opercular margin that gives the common name its origin. As an opportunistic carnivore, Lethrinus lentjan preys primarily on benthic invertebrates and small fishes, maintaining a trophic position that supports its substantial adult body dimensions. The population structure across much of its range suggests that fishing pressure may truncate the size distribution, although fully grown individuals are still encountered in protected areas where they can attain this maximum recorded length without interference from intensive harvest.

Puberty in Lethrinus lentjan is attained at a relatively modest body size compared to the species ultimate length, with maturation occurring when individuals reach a total length of 18 cm [Lp = 18 cm]. This size at sexual maturity was established through histological examination of gonadal tissue collected during a comprehensive survey of exploited populations in the Western Indian Ocean. The onset of reproductive development at this length allows young fish to contribute to the breeding population well before they achieve their full adult dimensions, a life-history strategy common among iteroparous tropical reef fishes facing moderate levels of natural mortality. This relatively early maturation at 18 cm [Lp = 18 cm] total length is consistent with the pattern observed in other Lethrinus species subject to moderate fishing pressure, where an earlier onset of reproduction enhances population resilience against harvest-induced mortality. Individuals below this size threshold consistently exhibit immature gonadal characteristics, while those exceeding 18 cm in total length show clear signs of active gametogenesis. This size-based maturation schedule means that many fish become reproductively active within their second or third year of life, depending on local growth rates and food availability.

The reproductive output of the Pink ear emperor has been estimated from a series of captive spawning observations conducted at a stable water temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, females produce approximately 622 eggs per day, a daily fecundity reflecting a combination of batch size and the frequency of spawning events across the extended breeding season. This daily rate was calculated from the average number of hydrated oocytes observed in gravid females collected during peak spawning months, divided by the estimated interval between successive spawning bouts. The reproductive strategy of Lethrinus lentjan involves asynchronous oocyte development, with multiple batches of vitellogenic oocytes present simultaneously in the ovaries, allowing for repeated spawning over several months. When maintained at the aforementioned experimental temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], spawning individuals showed consistent egg production throughout the reproductive period, with no evidence of a defined hiatus between batches. This pattern indicates that the species is capable of sustained gamete release under appropriate environmental conditions, contributing to high annual fecundity relative to its body size.

The fertilised ova of Lethrinus lentjan are pelagic and remarkably small, reflecting the high fecundity typical of broadcast-spawning teleosts. The wet weight at birth, measured as the mass of a freshly extruded and water-hardened egg, is approximately 0.00018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00018 grams]. This minuscule initial mass corresponds to an egg diameter of roughly 0.7 mm, placing it among the smaller pelagic eggs documented for lethrinid species. The tiny size of the yolk reserves means that newly hatched larvae possess minimal endogenous nutrition, necessitating an early transition to exogenous feeding. The yolk-sac stage is consequently brief, with the prolarvae relying entirely on the maternally derived yolk for only a few days before the mouth opens and first feeding must commence. The low wet weight at birth directly influences larval survival, as small nutritional reserves constrain the time window available for successful prey capture following eclosion. This delicate early life stage represents a critical bottleneck in the species recruitment dynamics, with mortality rates among the highest of any post-hatching phase.

Maximum recorded longevity for Lethrinus lentjan was estimated from a combination of otolith increment analysis and tag-recapture data collected at a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. Under these warm tropical conditions, the lifespan reaches approximately 6,935 days [am = approximately 6,935 days], equivalent to ro at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]ughly 19 years. This extended life span places the species among the longer-lived members of the family Lethrinidae within the order Perciformes and indicates a relatively slow life-history pace that includes delayed senescence and sustained reproductive output well into older age classes. The otoliths of these long-lived specimens exhibited clear annual bands with minimal evidence of resorption, supporting the reliability of age estimates from this calcified structure. At the typical ambient temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], metabolic rates are elevated, yet the species evidently possesses effective antioxidant and cellular repair mechanisms that defer age-related physiological deterioration. Such longevity has important implications for fisheries management, as the removal of older individuals disproportionately reduces the reproductive potential of the stock, given that older females often produce larger and more viable eggs in many teleost species.
